questions.q: Which annotation should you write for a task title?
questions.explain: TypeScript's basic types are lowercase: string, number, boolean. String with a capital S is JavaScript's wrapper object, which you almost never want.

questions.q: A task has priority = 2 and estimateHours = 0.5. Which types do they get?
questions.explain: TypeScript has one number type for whole numbers and decimals alike, just like JavaScript has one kind of number.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The annotations only describe the values; they do not change them. The program prints the same thing plain JavaScript would.

questions.q: Which type means exactly the same as string[]?
questions.explain: string[] and Array<string> are two spellings of "an array of strings". [string] is different: a tuple with exactly one string.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: tags is a normal string[], so push works. total only reads its readonly array: 0.5 + 2 + 1 is 3.5.

questions.q: Which line inside total does tsc reject?
questions.explain: A readonly array can be read in every way, but it has no methods that change it, such as push, pop or sort. reduce only reads.
options: Line 2: you cannot read from a readonly array
Line 4: length is not allowed on a readonly array

questions.q: Why would a function take readonly number[] instead of number[]?
questions.explain: readonly is a promise checked by the compiler: the function cannot call push, sort and so on. It does not freeze anything at runtime; the type is removed before running.
options: It makes the function run faster
It turns the array into a tuple
The caller can be sure the function leaves their array unchanged
It freezes the array at runtime with Object.freeze

questions.q: A function returns a pair: the number of open tasks and the number of done tasks. Which return type describes that fixed shape?
questions.explain: A tuple has a fixed length and a type for each position. The labels open and done are only documentation. number[] would allow any length.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: entry[1] is the string, so it can be uppercased. One flag is true, so done is 1 and open is 3 − 1 = 2. Destructuring takes the tuple apart in order.

questions.q: With const entry: [number, string] = [1, "Buy milk"];, which line does tsc accept?
questions.explain: Destructuring a tuple gives id: number and title: string. The others are errors: the tuple has no index 2, the positions are swapped, and entry[1] is a string, not a number.

questions.q: When does the lesson say an object is better than a tuple?
questions.explain: Tuples are fine for small, obvious pairs like [min, max]. With more positions, named properties are easier to read than remembering what index 4 means.
options: When the values are all numbers
When there are more than two or three positions
When the function returns two values

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The object type is written straight on the parameter. When done is false, the ternary adds an empty string, so only the second line gets " (done)".
options:
#1 Buy milk false
#2 Call Ada true

questions.q: With type Task = { id: number; title: string; done: boolean }, which line does tsc accept?
questions.explain: The order of properties does not matter. a is missing done, and b and c have properties the type does not know; in an object literal an extra property is an error, because it is almost always a typo.
options: const b: Task = { id: 2, titel: "Call Ada", done: false };
const c: Task = { id: 3, title: "Pay rent", done: false, tag: "home" };
const d: Task = { title: "Pay rent", done: true, id: 4 };

questions.q: With strict on, what is the type of task here?
questions.explain: find gives undefined when nothing matches, and TypeScript remembers that. The | makes a union: "a task, or undefined".

questions.q: After const task = tasks.find((t) => t.id === 2);, you write console.log(task.title);. What does tsc say?
questions.explain: This is strictNullChecks, switched on by strict. Without it, the program could crash with Cannot read properties of undefined, one of the most common JavaScript errors.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: No task has id 2, so the if branch runs and task?.title is undefined. ?? replaces both undefined and null, so the missing title and the null note both get the fallback text.

task 2 not found
Buy milk
(no title)
(no note)

task 2 not found
Buy milk
undefined
null

Buy milk
Buy milk
(no title)
(no note)

task 2 not found

questions.q: Inside if (task !== undefined) { ... }, TypeScript treats task as a Task, not Task | undefined. What is this called?
questions.explain: A check makes the type smaller: that is narrowing. The compiler follows your if, typeof and === checks to know which case you are in.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ?? uses the fallback only for null or undefined, so 0 ?? 1 keeps the 0. || also replaces falsy values like 0, which is usually a bug for numbers.

questions.q: The list is empty. What does this print?
questions.explain: ?. stops and gives undefined when the value on its left is missing, instead of crashing. Only the second expression has a ?? fallback, so only it prints none.
options: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'title')

questions.q: The lesson (and ZudoJS) uses a convention for undefined and null. Which one?
questions.explain: A property like note: string | null is always present, but may be deliberately empty. That is also how a database NULL column arrives in your code.
options: Both mean the same thing, so pick either at random
Never use null; it was removed from strict mode

questions.q: With the lesson's tsconfig.json, what is the type of tasks[0] when tasks is a Task[]?
questions.explain: Indexing an array gives the element type. Only the stricter noUncheckedIndexedAccess setting makes it Task | undefined. That is why the lesson writes tasks[0]?.title to be safe.
options: Task, even though the array might be empty

questions.q: This file passes tsc. What does it print?
questions.explain: any turns checking off, so tsc accepts toFixed, a number method, on a string. The mistake only shows at runtime, as a TypeError.
options:
BUY MILK
TypeError: input.toFixed is not a function

questions.q: What is the difference between any and unknown?
questions.explain: Both can hold any value. With any, every mistake gets through. With unknown, you must first check the value (for example with typeof), and then TypeScript narrows it.
options: They are two names for the same type
unknown turns checking off; any makes you check first
any turns checking off; unknown lets you do nothing until you check
unknown can only hold strings and numbers

questions.q: What does tsc say about this code?
questions.explain: The compiler goes by the type, not the value. For an unknown, you must check first, for example if (typeof input === "string").
options: Nothing: the value really is a string

questions.q: Which type should a function use for a request body that comes from outside the program?
questions.explain: Outside data could be anything, so be honest: unknown. The compiler then makes you check it. Typing it as Task or any would let bad data straight through.
options: The Task type, because that is what clients should send

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each typeof check narrows input in its branch. The number 3 becomes "3.00", and the object is neither a string nor a number.

questions.q: What does the return type void mean?
questions.explain: Functions that only print or save something return void. A function that never returns (it always throws) has the return type never.
options: The function returns, but without a useful value

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A void function has no return value, and in JavaScript calling it gives undefined. void is only a type; it does not exist at runtime.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: fail always throws, so the line after it never runs. String(error) gives the error's name and message.
options:
after fail
Error: database is down

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each status has its own case, so the default branch never runs. It is there only for the compiler: when every case is handled, status has type never there.

questions.q: A teammate adds "blocked" to type Status = "todo" | "doing" | "done" but does not update the switch with the const unreachable: never = status; default. What happens?
questions.explain: Now "blocked" can reach default, so status is not never there. The compiler points at the incomplete switch, even in a file the teammate never opened. This is an exhaustiveness check.
options: Nothing, until a blocked task reaches the switch at runtime
tsc reports Type '"blocked"' is not assignable to type 'never' at that line

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: task.estimate ?? 0 turns the null estimate into 0, so the sum is 3.5, not NaN. nextTask([]) is undefined, so ?. and ?? give the fallback text.

questions.q: This line fails with Object is possibly 'undefined'. Which fix is the one the lesson wants?
questions.explain: Handle the missing case: ?. gives undefined instead of crashing, and ?? picks the fallback. any, ! and turning off strict only silence the compiler; the crash would still happen.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: "2.5" becomes 2.5, which is not a whole number, so 0. true is neither a number nor a string, so n stays 0. "12" converts to 12.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With one number, it is both the smallest and the largest. The empty array returns early with undefined. Tuple labels like min are only documentation; at runtime it is a plain array.

questions.q: Finish average: return the average of the numbers, or 0 for an empty array. Do not change the array. The program should print 2.5 0.
questions.explain: Check for the empty array first, or you would divide 0 by 0 and get NaN. Reading a readonly array with for...of and length is allowed.

questions.q: Finish firstAndLast: return a tuple with the first and the last tag. The program should print home urgent.
questions.explain: Return an array literal with two strings: [tags[0], tags[tags.length - 1]]. The solution adds ?? "" so an empty array gives empty strings instead of undefined. The caller takes the tuple apart with destructuring.

questions.q: Finish titleOf: return the title of the task with that id, or not found. Do not use any or !. The program should print Buy milk and then not found.
questions.explain: find returns Task | undefined. ?.title reads the title only when a task was found, and ?? "not found" covers the missing case. An if check works too.

questions.q: Finish toCount. A number is returned as it is. A string such as "3" is converted with Number. Anything else, and any result that is not a whole number of 0 or more, gives 0. The program should print 4 3 0 0 0.
questions.explain: Check with typeof before using an unknown value; TypeScript narrows it in each branch. Number.isInteger rejects NaN (from "three") as well as decimals.

questions.q: Finish minMax: return a tuple [min, max], or undefined for an empty array. The program should print [ 1, 5 ] and then undefined.
questions.explain: Handle the empty case first; Math.min() of nothing is Infinity. Then spread the numbers into Math.min and Math.max.

questions.q: Finish priorityLabel with a switch and an exhaustiveness check in the default branch: "low" gives Later, "normal" gives Soon, "high" gives Now. The program should print Later Soon Now.
questions.explain: After three cases, priority is never in default, so const unreachable: never = priority compiles. If someone adds a fourth priority, that line becomes a type error.

questions.q: Finish noteLabel: return the note, or (no note) when it is null. An empty string "" is a real note and must be kept. The program should print call first|(no note)||.
questions.explain: ?? replaces only null and undefined. note || "(no note)" would also replace the empty string, which is wrong here.

questions.q: Finish describe for an unknown value: a string gives text: plus the string, a boolean gives yes or no, and anything else gives other. The program should print text: hi yes no other.
questions.explain: Each typeof check narrows value, so inside it you may use the value as a string or a boolean. Without a check, tsc refuses to use an unknown.

questions.q: Finish progress: return a tuple with the number of done tasks and the total number of tasks. The program should print 1/3 done.
questions.explain: filter does not change the array, so it is allowed on a readonly Task[]. The tuple type makes the order clear: done first, total second.

questions.q: Some tasks have no estimate yet (null). Finish totalEstimate so it adds up the hours and counts a missing estimate as 0. The program should print 3.5.
questions.explain: hours += task.estimate is a type error, because the estimate may be null. task.estimate ?? 0 handles that case, and the result is a plain number.
